title: Go tutorial: types, slices, structs, goroutines and errors — cv.cm
description: Learn Go in one page: install Go and run Hello world, types, loops, functions, slices and maps, structs and interfaces, goroutines and channels, and errors.
answer: Go (often called Golang) is a simple, compiled, statically typed language from Google, built for fast builds, easy concurrency and reliable servers. Install Go, write a `main` package and run it with `go run hello.go`. The core ideas are a small set of types, slices and maps, structs with methods, implicit interfaces, goroutines and channels for concurrency, and errors returned as ordinary values.

sections.h: What Go is and what it is used for
body: Go was designed at Google by Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike and Ken Thompson and released as open source in 2009. It compiles to a single static binary, starts fast, has a garbage collector and a rich standard library for networking. It is used for cloud infrastructure and command-line tools: Docker, Kubernetes, Terraform and Prometheus are written in Go, and many companies use it for web APIs and microservices. The language is deliberately small, so code from different teams looks similar.

sections.h: Install Go and run Hello, world
body: Download Go from go.dev/dl and check it with `go version`. Create a folder, start a module, and add `main.go`:

body.code:
go mod init example.com/hello
go run .
# Hello, world
go build     # produces a standalone binary named hello

body: Execution starts at `func main` in `package main`. Run `gofmt` (or `go fmt`) to format code; all Go code uses the same style, with tabs for indentation in real source files.

Declare variables with `var name type = value`, or inside functions with the short form `name := value`, which infers the type. Variables that are not assigned get a zero value: `0`, `""`, `false` or `nil`.
Go never converts between numeric types implicitly, and the compiler rejects unused variables and unused imports.
There are no parentheses around conditions, and braces are required. `for` is the only loop keyword: it covers classic, while-style and range loops. Functions can return several values.
A slice is a growable view of an array and is the everyday list type. A map is a hash table. A struct groups named fields, and methods are functions with a receiver.
Iteration order over a map is deliberately random; sort the keys if you need a stable order. Names that start with a capital letter (`Point`, `Add`) are exported from the package.
An interface lists method signatures. A type satisfies an interface simply by having those methods; there is no `implements` keyword.
Go also has generics (since Go 1.18), for example `func Max[T int | float64](a, b T) T`, which you will use mostly through library functions such as those in the `slices` and `maps` packages.

A goroutine is a lightweight thread started with the `go` keyword; a program can run many thousands of them. Goroutines communicate through channels, which pass values safely between them. `sync.WaitGroup` waits for a group of goroutines to finish.
`defer` schedules a call to run when the surrounding function returns, which is how Go code closes files and unlocks mutexes. Use `go run -race .` to detect data races while developing.

Go has no exceptions for ordinary failures. A function that can fail returns an `error` as its last result, and the caller checks it right away. Wrap errors with `%w` to add context while keeping the original error inspectable with `errors.Is`.
`panic` and `recover` exist, but they are reserved for programming errors and truly unexpected states, not for normal error handling.

sections.h: A small complete program: a tiny web server
body: With only the standard library, this program serves JSON over HTTP. Run it with `go run .` and open `http://localhost:8080/hello?name=Ann`.
The text after each field type is a struct tag that sets the JSON key name. Each request is handled in its own goroutine automatically.

body.note: Writing to a `nil` map panics. A map declared with `var m map[string]int` must be created with `make(map[string]int)` or a literal before you assign to it.

ul: Ignoring errors with `_`. Check every returned `error` unless you are sure it cannot matter.
Expecting `append` to change the original slice in place; always use the result, as in `s = append(s, x)`.
Starting goroutines and letting `main` return before they finish. Wait with `sync.WaitGroup` or channels.
Using a value receiver when the method must modify the struct; use a pointer receiver such as `func (p *Point)`.

body: Take the interactive Tour of Go, then read Effective Go and the standard library documentation at pkg.go.dev. Learn `go test` for unit tests and benchmarks, the `context` package for timeouts and cancellation, and modules for dependencies.

faq.q: Is it called Go or Golang?
faq.a: The official name is Go. "Golang" comes from the old website address golang.org and is still used as a search term.
Partly. Go has methods and interfaces but no classes or inheritance; you build types by embedding structs and composing small interfaces.
For most CPU-bound work, yes, because Go compiles to native machine code and has static types. Python can still be fast when the heavy work happens inside libraries written in C.

faq.q: What is the difference between a goroutine and a thread?
faq.a: A goroutine is managed by the Go runtime and starts with a small stack that grows as needed. The runtime schedules many goroutines onto a few operating system threads, so goroutines are much cheaper to create.
